parts.label: Classify
parts.title: Classify the use and your role before listing duties
parts.body:
The EU AI Act attaches different duties to prohibited practices, high-risk systems, specified transparency uses, and providers of general-purpose AI models. Classification depends on the system's intended purpose and the organization's role. A company using a supplier's recruitment screener is generally assessing deployer duties; a company placing its own system on the EU market may be a provider. Contract labels alone do not settle this. Legal counsel should examine the actual product and supply chain, including any material change or rebranding.

Start an inventory row for each EU use: purpose, people affected, geography, provider and deployer, model supplier, data, and downstream decision. Check prohibited uses first. Then examine whether Annex I product rules or Annex III use cases apply. Recruitment and worker management are among Annex III areas; ordinary office text drafting does not become high-risk simply because it uses a capable model. Assess Article 50 transparency duties and any general-purpose model-provider role separately.

The AI Act is law, while NIST and OECD frameworks offer voluntary governance methods. The GDPR remains a separate analysis when personal data is processed. An EU recruitment project therefore needs both AI Act classification and GDPR work on lawful processing, rights, roles, and transfers. A classification memo should cite the actual provisions and record counsel's conclusion and reassessment trigger.

example.title: A cross-border recruiting tool
example.body: A group procures software to rank Paris applicants and also uses it in Toronto. The EU team records its likely Annex III recruitment use and deployer role, then asks counsel to confirm any exception or relevant obligations. The Canadian team separately identifies applicable privacy and employment rules. The supplier's claim of 'GDPR compliance' does not answer either classification question.

exercise.title: Create a classification memo
exercise.body: For a hypothetical recruitment screener, write the intended use, EU role, likely AI Act category, data-processing roles, source provisions to verify, unresolved facts, counsel owner, and trigger for revisiting classification. Do the same for a simple internal drafting assistant and compare.

parts.label: Plan
parts.title: Build a dated obligation register
parts.body:
The AI Act applies in stages, and amendments can change dates. As of October 2026, the Commission's implementation timeline shows AI literacy and initial prohibitions from February 2025, general-purpose AI model provisions from August 2025, and many transparency rules from August 2026. It lists Annex III high-risk rules for December 2027 and Annex I product-related high-risk rules for August 2028 after the Digital Omnibus amendments. It also lists a further December 2026 milestone. Verify the live official timeline and consolidated legislation whenever a release or board decision depends on a date.

For every applicable duty, keep a row with the legal provision, system and role, effective date, accountable owner, required evidence, readiness status, and next check date. Separate enacted law from guidance, voluntary codes, and proposals. A deadline in a presentation becomes dangerous when a product team cannot tell which version and role it came from.

Plan for lead time, not merely the legal date. High-risk provider obligations can require risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency to deployers, human oversight, and quality management. A deployer has a different set of duties. Procurement terms must provide the information the deploying organization needs. Ask counsel and the supplier for a role-specific matrix before committing to launch.

example.title: A change log catches a false assumption
example.body: A team has an old slide that says all high-risk duties began in August 2026. The regulatory owner compares it with the Commission's current timeline, records the applicable Annex III date and amendment source, and updates the obligation register. The project still does the preparatory work now rather than postponing its risk controls.

exercise.title: Make a regulatory calendar
exercise.body: Create five register rows for one EU use: provision, role, effective date with official source and access date, evidence, and responsible owner. Add a quarterly review and a trigger for amendments or changed use. Have counsel validate the classification before treating the rows as obligations.

parts.label: Compare
parts.title: Keep EU and Canadian analyses distinct
parts.body:
A global policy can share inventory fields, risk assessment, testing, and incident processes. Legal applicability still follows the use, organization, people, and jurisdiction. In Canada, PIPEDA governs many private-sector commercial activities, while substantially similar provincial private-sector laws can apply in Alberta, British Columbia, and Québec. Health, employment, and public-sector settings may have additional or different provincial and federal rules. Ask privacy counsel to map the actual entity and data flow.

Canada's federal Directive on Automated Decision-Making applies to federal departments in its defined scope. It is a useful public-sector example, not a general statute governing every Canadian company. A private employer in Toronto should not copy its impact-level duties into a legal register as though they bind it automatically. It may borrow the idea of a documented impact assessment as governance practice.

In the EU, the AI Act and GDPR address different aspects of a system. An AI Act category does not replace lawful basis, minimization, processor arrangements, data subject rights, or transfer assessment under GDPR. The CAIO can maintain a common global control baseline and add a jurisdiction overlay that names counsel, local owner, and required evidence. A single label such as 'compliant in Europe and Canada' conceals these distinctions.

example.title: One tool, two overlays
example.body: An interview-summary service runs in Berlin and Montréal. The group uses one technical evaluation and incident runbook, while EU counsel reviews GDPR and AI Act use classification and Québec counsel reviews the provincial privacy and employment setting. Procurement records data locations and subprocessors for both.

exercise.title: Draft an overlay table
exercise.body: For Berlin and Montréal deployments, list common controls and separate EU and Canadian legal questions. Name the facts you need from procurement and local teams. Mark the federal Canadian automated-decision directive as inapplicable unless the defined federal institution and use are present.

sources: Office of the Privacy Commissioner: summary of Canadian privacy laws
European Data Protection Board: AI models and GDPR opinion

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Run regulatory scanning as a product process
parts.body:
Assign one owner to monitor the official EU AI Act Service Desk, Commission guidance, consolidated law, and relevant national authorities; assign local owners for Canadian privacy and sector rules. Give each change an intake record: published date, legal status, affected roles and systems, interpretation, action, decision owner, and deadline. Counsel validates legal conclusions; product and control owners execute changes. Keep the previous interpretation and reason for amendment so a board can see what changed.

Prioritize a change by affected population, system impact, enforcement date, and lead time. A new disclosure duty may require interface design and translation. A change in high-risk classification may require supplier evidence and revised contract terms. A regulatory update that does not apply should still get a short rationale and a review trigger.

At each release, ask the regulatory owner to confirm the register's access date and applicable rules. Add a recurring review during operation and after material changes in purpose, geography, model, or autonomy. This is an operating habit that survives a moving timeline. The executive report should contain the few decisions needing resources or risk acceptance, not a dump of regulatory headlines.

example.title: A change with a visible owner
example.body: An EU transparency clarification affects a public chatbot's disclosure. Legal logs the source and effective scope; product designs the notice; accessibility checks the interaction; the release owner tests the display in all supported languages. The CAIO sees the readiness date and unresolved decision in the portfolio register.

exercise.title: Run a mock update
exercise.body: Assume an official authority publishes a new interpretation relevant to one of your AI uses. Write an intake record with legal status, affected inventory IDs, owner, decision required, verification source, test, and communication plan. Show what would make you defer a release.

sources: European Commission AI Act Service Desk
Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
